Company’s Response:  
 
(i) 
The Board provides ongoing guidance to management through a quarterly review of 
management accounts, key financial ratios, cash flow positions and the progress of material 
projects, as well as at half-yearly Board meetings and through ad-hoc meeting discussions with 
management. Key areas of focus include improving the collection of trade receivables, 
strengthening credit control and collection procedures and optimising payment terms with 
suppliers, where commercially practicable. 
 
Management is required to monitor working capital movements and operating cash flows on a 
regular basis, identify significant variances between reported profits and operating cash flows, 
and implement appropriate measures to address any adverse trends. The Board will continue 
to review the Group’s working capital position and cash flow forecasts as part of its ongoing 
oversight of the Group’s financial performance and liquidity. 
 
In relation to working capital efficiency, Management will monitor key indicators, including trade 
receivables collection days, inventory holding days, trade payables payment days and the cash 
conversion cycle. Appropriate targets will be assessed against the Group’s historical 
performance, business and project specific requirements and prevailing market conditions. 
 

 
2 
 
The Board recognises that the timing of cash conversion may be affected by project milestones, 
customer payment cycles and other operational factors. Accordingly, the Group will continue to 
focus on improving working capital efficiency and strengthening operating cash flow generation.  
The Board and Management will monitor progress closely, with the objective of achieving 
sustainable and healthy operating cash flows as the Group’s working capital position improves. 
 
(ii) 
Contract assets primarily relate to the Group’s right to consideration for work completed but not 
billed at the reporting date on contracts and any impairment losses recognised in the reporting 
year. The contract assets are transferred to the receivables when the rights become 
unconditional. This usually occurs when the work is certified by the customers and the Group 
invoices the customers. The increase in contract assets of S$15.0 million or 203.7% was mainly

contract assets were as a result of normal certification and billing cycles according to the specific 
projects’ milestones

(i)

(ii)

pricing and size of the share buybacks, and how did they satisfy themselves that the 
repurchases were in the interests of the company and its shareholders as a whole?  
 
Company’s Response:  
 
(i) 
The Board wishes to highlight that the placement exercise and subsequent share buybacks 
occurred at different times, taking into account the Group’s business requirements, financial 
position, and prevailing market conditions. 
 
The placement exercise completed in December 2025 raised net proceeds of approximately 
S$2.11 million to strengthen the Group’s working capital position and support its ongoing 
projects, which were used for the repayment of trade facilities to pay suppliers and 
subcontractors. The placement price of S$0.22 per share represented a premium of 
approximately 3.14% to the volume-weighted average price of S$0.2133 per share on 21 
November 2025. The exercise attracted prominent institutional investors, including Lion Global 
Investors limited (as investment manager for and on behalf of its clients), ICH Synergrowth Fund 
and Ginko-AGT Global Growth Fund. 
 
Since the placement, the Group has continued to achieve positive business and financial 
developments. For FY2026, the Group recorded its strongest financial performance to date, 
with net profit more than tripling S$8.1 million, with its order book at S$106.2 million as at 30 
June 2026. 
 
The Board believes that the improvement in the Company’s share price reflects the progress 
made in executing its business strategy and the improvement in its financial performance. The 
subsequent share buybacks since 25 March 2026 were undertaken pursuant to the Share Buy 
Back Mandate approved by shareholders at the Annual General Meeting held on 30 October 
2025, with the objective of enhancing long-term shareholder value. At the time of the placement, 
additional capital was required to support working capital and project execution. Following 
stronger than expected financial performance, the Board assessed that the Group had sufficient 
capital resources for its operational and growth requirements. Accordingly, the Group 
commenced share buybacks as a capital management initiative. In considering its capital 
allocation priorities, the Board seeks to balance maintaining sufficient working capital to support 
ongoing projects, pursuing business growth opportunities, and returning value to shareholders.  
 
The Board remains committed to prudent capital management, and believes that the placement 
exercise and subsequent share buybacks serve different purposes within the Group’s broader 
objective of delivering sustainable long-term shareholder value. 

 
4 
 
 
(ii)  
The Company’s share buybacks were undertaken pursuant to the Share Buy Back Mandate 
approved by shareholders at the Annual General Meeting held on 30 October 2025, and in 
accordance with the applicable regulatory requirements under the Companies Act 1967 and the 
Catalist Rules.  
 
The Share Buy Back Mandate authorises the Directors to repurchase shares within the 
prescribed limits, including a maximum purchase price of 105% of the average closing price of 
the shares over the preceding five market days for on-market purchases. 
 
As part of the Board’s oversight responsibilities, the Independent Directors considered the 
Group’s financial position, working capital requirements, prevailing market conditions and 
ongoing business commitments when approving the budget for the Management to execute the 
share buybacks within the prescribed limits. Having satisfied themselves that the share 
buybacks would not materially affect the Group’s financial flexibility, ability to meet its obligations 
or pursue growth opportunities, the Independent Directors were of the view that the share 
buybacks, undertaken in accordance with the Share Buy Back Mandate, were in the interests 
of the Company and its shareholders as a whole and would support long-term shareholder 
value.

Company’s response to Q1(i) 
The Group does not manufacture grating. It is an authorised distributor for an 
established German grating manufacturer, and supplies its products according to client 

specifications for offshore and marine projects, where clients place emphasis on 
compliance with project standards, consistent quality and on-time delivery. The 
Group’s offering combines the manufacturer’s product quality and certifications with 
local project support, including advising clients on product selection, coordinating 
materials to meet project specifications, arranging cutting and fitting where required, 
and managing logistics and delivery schedules. The Group’s own storage yard and 
logistics capabilities allow it to coordinate the storage, handling and delivery of 
materials in line with clients’ project requirements, which is particularly relevant to 
offshore and marine projects with demanding specifications and delivery schedules. 
The offshore and marine grating contracts secured in FY2026 reflected a combination 
of product quality, competitive pricing, delivery reliability, logistics capabilities and 
established customer relationships, rather than price alone. Repeat orders from an 
established client show that our quality and delivery record has been accepted on prior 
projects. Pricing remains competitive, and the Group continues to tender selectively for 
contracts with better margins rather than competing on price. 
The Group has maintained established customer relationships in the oil and gas 
industry since 2015, spanning more than a decade, and has developed a strong 
understanding of clients’ technical requirements, operational expectations and project 
delivery schedules. We believe this industry experience, our operational infrastructure 
and our ability to consistently meet clients’ requirements are our competitive 
advantages, as offshore and marine clients generally prefer proven suppliers. In 
addition, as the Group also provides transport, security and manpower services, it often 
has existing relationships with clients across more than one business segment. These 
touch points give the Group a better understanding of clients’ wider operational needs 
and allow it to offer complementary services alongside grating supply. Having said that, 
the market is competitive, and these advantages must be sustained through continued 
operational performance, strong supplier relationships and competitive pricing. The 
Group will continue to focus on sustainable margins while strengthening existing client 
relationships and broadening its client base. 
(ii) 
Transport services: Given the significant increase in diesel prices, how was the 
transport services segment able to improve its profitability in FY2026? Can 
management quantify the respective contributions from improved vehicle 
utilisation, pricing, changes in customer or service mix, and cost control? 
Company’s response to Q1(ii) 
Transport services revenue grew 31.8% to $7.31 million and gross profit grew 58.4% 
to $1.48 million, with gross margin improving from about 16.9% to 20.3%. 
The improvement came mainly from higher vehicle utilisation, as additional contracts 
were served largely with the existing fleet, together with continued fleet optimisation, 
better route planning and stronger demand from commercial clients. As a result, 
revenue grew faster than the segment’s main operating costs. Driver salaries and 
related costs increased by about 12.4%, while repair and maintenance and insurance 
costs increased by about 2.4% and 2.6% respectively. Depreciation decreased by 
about $137,000, as more of the fleet became fully depreciated while remaining in 
service. 
To support new contracts, the Group also made greater use of subcontracted transport 
services, with subcontractor costs increasing from about $0.86 million to $1.79 million. 

Fuel expense increased from about $0.63 million to $0.85 million, reflecting higher 
diesel prices and the higher level of activity. Despite these increases, cost of sales 
grew by 26.4%, below revenue growth of 31.8%, resulting in the higher gross margin. 
These figures show the principal cost movements. However, the effects of vehicle 
utilisation, pricing and changes in customer or service mix operate together and are 
not tracked separately in a way that allows their respective contributions to be reliably 
quantified. Diesel cost remains a key sensitivity, and the Group takes fuel prices into 
account when pricing new and renewed contracts. The Group will continue to focus on 
securing contracts with healthy margins and managing operating costs prudently. 
(iii) 
Investment properties: The group operates two dormitories with a combined capacity 
of 707 beds. What were the occupancy rates as at 30 June 2026 and the latest 
available date (such as 30 September 2026)? How did actual occupancy rates 
and average rates compare with management’s projections when the 
investments were planned?

comprise industrial space that is leased to tenants or used by the Group for its own 
operations, with about half of the space repositioned as a workers’ dormitory. The 
dormitories at Amethyst House and Beryl House have 299 beds and 408 beds 
respectively. As at 30 June 2026 and 30 September 2026, both dormitories were 
operating at close to full occupancy of above 95%, with vacant beds mainly arising 
from the turnover between tenant check-outs and check-ins. 
Amethyst House has operated at consistently high occupancy. Beryl House received 
its FEDA licence in mid-May 2026 and reached close to full occupancy faster than 
anticipated. 
When the investments were evaluated, the Board’s assessment allowed for a ramp-up 
period after licensing before occupancy stabilises. Actual occupancy and average bed 
rates have been ahead of those expectations. The investment properties segment 
turned from a gross loss of $0.50 million in FY2025 to a gross profit of $0.85 million in

space at both properties. The industrial space at Beryl House has been leased to 
tenants since the Group took over the property in December 2024, but its dormitory 
began operations only after it received its FEDA licence in mid-May 2026. The Beryl 
House dormitory therefore contributed only about six weeks of operations in FY2026, 
and its full contribution is expected from FY2027

The Group’s businesses are mainly manpower-driven, and its scale depends on its 
workforce rather than its PPE. The carrying amount of PPE also understates the assets

Security services are delivered entirely by the Group’s own employees. Manpower 
services are also delivered mainly by the Group’s own employees, with subcontractors 
engaged to support peak-period deployment. Transport services use the Group’s own 
fleet and drivers, supplemented by subcontracted capacity to support new contracts. 
Engineering services use the Group’s own scaffold equipment and workers, with 
subcontractors engaged for specialised scopes and peak workloads. 
Our own employees remain the main delivery channel. In FY2026, employee benefits 
expense in cost of sales was $17.72 million, compared with subcontractor costs of 
$2.43 million. Subcontractors therefore accounted for about 12% of these combined 
costs, up from about 5% in FY2025. The increase was mainly in transport services, 
which accounted for about three-quarters of FY2026 subcontractor costs. 
Subcontracted capacity allowed the Group to mobilise new transport contracts 
promptly while it assesses whether their volume and duration justify further investment 
in its own fleet. The balance related mainly to engineering services, for specialised 
scopes and peak workloads, and to manpower services, for peak-period deployment. 
This approach allowed the Group to grow revenue without committing to additional 
fixed costs ahead of demand. 
To safeguard quality, reliability and margins, subcontractors are engaged from an 
approved list based on capability, safety record and past performance. Subcontracted 

costs are priced into each project and project margins are reviewed against budget. 
Subcontracted work is supervised by our own project and site personnel, who remain 
accountable to the client. 
As at 30 June 2026, the group does not carry inventory.

Is this consistent with the group’s normal operating model, or does it reflect the 
timing of project procurement and delivery? For the offshore and marine grating 
contracts, who bears the cost and risk of procuring and holding materials, and

Yes, this is consistent with the Group’s normal project-based operating model. The 
Group does not generally hold stock for resale. Materials are procured against 
confirmed orders and allocated to specific projects based on their technical 
specifications and delivery requirements. The inventory of $0.27 million as at 30 June 
2025 comprised materials which, following a review of its operating requirements in 
FY2026, the Group decided to retain for use in its own operations. These were 
therefore reclassified to property, plant and equipment. 
For the offshore and marine grating contracts, the Group procures materials from its 
German manufacturer against the client’s confirmed purchase orders and bears the 
procurement, holding and delivery risk until the materials are delivered to the client, 
subject to the agreed contract terms. This includes receiving the materials in bulk and 
breaking bulk at the Group’s own storage yard before delivery to the client’s site. This 
risk is mitigated by ordering only against confirmed orders from a reputable, long-
standing client, as described in our response to Q1(i), and by coordinating delivery 
schedules and closely monitoring project requirements. As the client pays upon 
delivery, working capital is required mainly for materials and labour between 
procurement and client payment. This is funded from internal resources, supported by 
the credit terms extended by the Group’s supplier, which shorten the period for which 
the Group funds the materials itself. The working capital required for these contracts is 
therefore modest and has been met from the Group’s operating cash flows, which 
amounted to $5.34 million in FY2026. The Group also maintains a disciplined approach 
to project selection and procurement commitments

hurdle rates does the board apply when approving new equipment purchases?  
 
Company’s Response: 
 
The average utilisation rate of 57% (FY2025: 54%) is a fleet-level figure across more than 600 cranes of 
very different types and capacities, from lorry cranes to the Group’s 2,200-tonne crawler crane, and it varies 
with mobilisation schedules, capacity limits, location and other operational factors. Management therefore 
assesses utilisation and returns by asset and by market rather than at fleet level. One large crane that is 
well utilised can contribute more than many smaller units with spare capacity. 
 
In deciding where additional capacity is justified, management considers: 
 
 
Cross-hire: where the Group repeatedly hires equipment from third parties to meet demand in a 
particular class, this points to a capacity gap. Cross-hire costs were elevated in FY2025 and FY2026, 
reflecting the strength of demand. In FY2026, overlapping project timelines also required the Group to 
hire in equipment to meet customers’ schedules and avoid delays. Some cross-hire is a normal part of 
the business, allowing the Group to take on work beyond its own fleet at any one time. 
 
 
Pipeline and customer requirements: the projects being tendered, particularly those requiring 
integrated solutions, where customers look for an asset-backed provider able to commit the equipment 
needed. 
 
 
Market capacity: in some size classes the market already has ample capacity and hiring in is more 
economical than owning. The Group concentrates its own investment on specialised and higher-capacity 
equipment. 
 
 
Fleet renewal: the fleet is renewed on a rolling basis as equipment reaches the end of its working life, 
and part of each year’s capital expenditure replaces older units. 
 
The Group also recycles capital, divesting underutilised units and redeploying the capital released. In 
FY2026, investment in property, plant and equipment of $53.5 million compared with a depreciation charge 
of $35.7 million. 
 
Proposals for new equipment are evaluated on their expected returns, cash flows and utilisation, and on 
downside scenarios, against the Group’s cost of capital. Return on equity has improved in each of the past 
four years, from 4.0% in FY2022 to 7.0% in FY2026. 
 
Q1 (iv) How confident is management in the sustained demand for heavy lift and haulage, especially 
in the key Singapore market? How has the board stress-tested the group’s resilience under a severe 
global downturn resulting in a material decline in demand across its key markets?  
 
Company’s Response: 
 
The Building and Construction Authority projects total construction demand of $47 billion to $53 billion in 
2026 and $39 billion to $46 billion a year from 2027 to 2030, anchored by major projects such as Changi 
Airport Terminal 5. Over the longer term, the plans announced at the National Day Rally in August 2026 to 

4 
 
connect several smaller islands south of Jurong Island into a new western island may create further 
opportunities. Demand from the semiconductor, data centre and biopharmaceutical sectors adds to this 
pipeline. Project activity can nonetheless vary from year to year, depending on the timing of contract awards 
and construction schedules. 
 
The business is nonetheless cyclical, and the Group has been through a severe downturn before. That 
experience shapes how the Group is run today: 
 
 
Balance sheet: as at 30 June 2026 the Group had cash and bank deposits of $86.6 million, net gearing 
of 9.5% and shareholders’ funds of $341.6 million. 
 
 
Diversification: the Group serves more than 300 customers a month across a range of sectors and 
markets, and no single customer accounted for more than 10% of revenue in FY2026. Contracted project 
work accounts for less than half of revenue, so the Group is not locked into long-term contracts priced 
on assumptions that may no longer hold. 
 
 
Flexibility: capital expenditure can be deferred, cross-hired equipment released and owned equipment 
redeployed across the Group’s markets as conditions change. 
 
While the Board does not conduct a separate formal stress test, the Group’s resilience is monitored through 
its financial planning and control processes, which are reported to the Board and include: 
 
 
Annual budgeting: the Group prepares an annual budget setting out its financial plan for the year. 
 
 
Variance analysis: actual results are compared with the budget periodically, and significant variances 
are reviewed. 
 
 
Forecasting: forecasts are updated periodically during the year to reflect changes in market conditions. 
Where forecasts fall below budget, management can respond, for example by deferring capital 
expenditure. 
 
 
Fleet utilisation: the Board reviews fleet utilisation quarterly against internal targets. 
 
 
Capital expenditure: major capital expenditure is reviewed against forecast cash flows and available 
funding before it is approved. 
 
 
Liquidity and capital structure: operating cash flows and liquidity are monitored closely, adequate 
cash and bank deposits are maintained, and the capital structure and gearing are reviewed regularly. 
Headroom under banking facilities and compliance with loan covenants are also monitored. 
 
 
Credit control: customers are subject to credit reviews and credit limits and, where practicable, those 
of lower credit standing transact on cash terms or make advance payments. 
 
The Enterprise Risk Management Committee, overseen by the Audit Committee, monitors market and 
business risks, and the Board receives assurance each year on the adequacy and effectiveness of the 
Group’s risk management and internal control systems. In FY2025, the Group also performed its first 
climate scenario analysis under IFRS S2, which considered the transition risks under a below-2°C 
scenario and the physical risks under a 4°C scenario.

Q2 (i) What specific outcome does management expect from the Enterprise Singapore Scale-Up 
programme?  
 
Company’s Response: 
 
The Group joined Enterprise Singapore’s Scale-Up programme during FY2026. The programme runs in 
two phases, a strategy phase followed by an acceleration phase. The Group is now in the acceleration 
phase, which is expected to be completed around the end of 2026. Through the programme, management 
is working with consultants to review the Group’s strategy against international best practice and to plan its 
growth over the medium term. 
 
The outcomes management expects from the programme are: 
 
 
a sharper growth strategy, with clearer choices on the markets, sectors and services the Group will 
prioritise in Singapore and the region; 
 
 
stronger capabilities to support regional growth, including a unified commercial team across Singapore 
and the region, integrated projects capabilities coordinated at Group level, with project execution 
supported by the respective operating business units, and fleet operations, safety and procurement 
managed at Group level; and 
 
 
a more structured approach to evaluating strategic investments and acquisitions that complement the 
Group’s core capabilities, including opportunities that strengthen the Group’s position outside 
Singapore.

returns on the Group’s assets.

overseas market.  
 
Q2 (ii) Given the group’s existing overseas experience, what are the principal barriers preventing it 
from establishing a larger and more sustainable presence outside Singapore? To what extent do 
these reflect external constraints, such as competition and market access, versus internal 
limitations in management bandwidth, local capabilities or willingness and ability to commit 
capital? At this stage of the group’s growth, how critical is regional expansion to its longer-term 
growth prospects?  
 
Company’s Response: 
 
Regional expansion is important to the Group’s long-term growth. Singapore remains the core market, 
where the Group’s fleet, engineering depth and customer relationships are greatest, but it is a relatively 
small market. The Group sees its overseas markets as a second engine of growth, extending its 
addressable market and diversifying its earnings. 
 
Singapore’s share of revenue rose to 77% in FY2026, from 73% in FY2025, mainly because Singapore 
revenue grew by $25.6 million on strong demand. Overseas revenue was $43.0 million, against $44.4 
million in FY2025: growth in India and Brunei was offset mainly by lower revenue from Malaysia, where a 
large one-off project in FY2025 was not repeated, and from the Middle East, where the pace of project 
execution moderated amid regional tensions. 
 
The constraints on building a larger overseas presence are both external and internal: 
 
 
External: heavy lifting is a local business in each market, with established local competitors, pricing 
pressure and local regulatory and licensing requirements. Project demand is uneven and, in some 
markets, exposed to political and geopolitical developments. The strength of the Singapore dollar has 
also given rise to foreign exchange losses, mainly on the intercompany balances through which 
overseas operations are funded; the Group’s net currency exchange loss was $3.9 million in FY2026. 
 
 
Internal: equipment can be moved between markets, but experienced people cannot be moved as 
easily. The main internal constraints are the availability of experienced local management and technical 
personnel, and the need to balance capital and equipment deployment between Singapore and the 
overseas markets. Building local teams that meet the Group’s safety and execution standards takes 
time. The new operating model described in (i) above is intended to strengthen Group-wide coordination 
and international business development capabilities. 
 
The Group’s approach overseas is long term. In markets such as India, it focuses on engineered, higher-
capacity lifts, where its fleet and expertise give it an advantage, rather than on the mass market. It has 
invested in TWC India, TWC Thailand and TWC Saudi Arabia over many years, acquired assets from 
Mammoet in Thailand in 2023 to extend its capabilities there, and in August 2026 incorporated a subsidiary 
in Papua New Guinea. The Group will continue to evaluate investments and acquisitions that complement 
its core capabilities or expand its regional presence, each assessed with financial discipline and due regard 
to execution and integration risks. 
 

7 
 
 
Q2 (iii) Thailand: What progress has management made, if any, under its strategic alliance with 
Mammoet?  
 
Company’s Response: 
 
The arrangement announced on 15 December 2023 has centred on the acquisition of transportation, heavy 
haulage and heavy lifting equipment from Mammoet, which has been integrated into TWC Thailand’s fleet, 
together with selected personnel. This has extended TWC Thailand’s capability to larger and more complex 
projects. It now offers an integrated suite of services spanning heavy lifting, heavy haulage, ballasting, 
weighing, skidding, and load-in and load-out, and in FY2026 it extended into data centre work. 
 
In June 2026, TWC Thailand completed the Group’s heaviest module load-out to date, moving a module 
of approximately 4,500 tonnes on self-propelled modular transporters for the Pluto T1 Scarborough pre-
assembled unit fabrication project. Revenue from Thailand was $11.2 million in FY2026, broadly stable 
against $11.4 million in FY2025. 
 
Q2 (iv) India: Several long-running engagements reached completion during the year: Indian Oil 
Corporation’s Panipat refinery in July 2025, Nayara Refinery in Gujarat in February 2026, and the 
Numaligarh Refinery in Assam and Indian Oil Corporation’s Baroda refinery in May 2026. With these major 
engagements completed, what replacement project(s) has the group secured or entered into 
advanced negotiations for in India? In the absence of sufficient replacement projects, does 
management expect revenue from India to decline, and by how much?  
 
Company’s Response: 
 
India was the Group’s largest overseas market in FY2026, with revenue of $15.4 million, or 8% of Group 
revenue (FY2025: $11.9 million). The Group’s work in India is project-based. Individual engagements run 
for months or years and are replaced through new tenders, so completions are a normal part of the business 
cycle. Work continues at the Talcher Fertiliser Plant in Odisha and at the Tata semiconductor facility in 
Dholera, and during FY2026 TWC India also launched one of the heaviest precast portal beams on the 
Mumbai–Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail Corridor. 
 
The Group continues to regard India as an important market with long-term opportunities in the refinery, 
petrochemical, energy and industrial infrastructure sectors. 
 
As several major projects have reached completion, the Group is actively pursuing new opportunities to 
replenish its project pipeline and sustain its presence in the market. These efforts include maintaining 
relationships with existing customers, engaging potential new customers and evaluating opportunities 
where the Group’s specialised heavy lifting and engineering capabilities provide a competitive advantage. 
 
Given the project-based nature of the business, revenue contributions from India may fluctuate between 
financial years, depending on the timing of project awards, commencement and execution. The Group will 
continue to adopt a disciplined approach to project selection, resource deployment and capital 
commitments. 
 
Management remains focused on developing a sustainable project pipeline and strengthening the Group’s 
longer-term competitive position in India.

Response: 
 
Australia and New Zealand differ significantly in market size and growth opportunities. Australia 
has a substantially larger population, generally providing a larger market and greater 
opportunities for expansion across multiple urban centres. Whilst both markets are competitive 
and mature, the opportunities in Australia are more diverse. Its larger consumer base and wider 
geographical reach provide the Group with greater opportunities to expand its brand portfolio, 

2 
 
reach new customers and strengthen its market presence. Considering amongst others, the 
above factors, the Group focuses more of its resources to support its geographical presence in 
Australia. Focusing a stronger presence in a particular geographical market allows the Group a 
greater potential for central kitchen economies of scale. A broader brand portfolio also provides 
greater opportunities for expansion and reduces reliance on any single brand segment. 
 
The Group operates 12 brands and 131 outlets in Australia across various segments, compared 
with 4 brands and 38 outlets in New Zealand, of which 32 of them are Gong Cha outlets.  
 
Management will continue to pursue sustainable growth in both markets utilising a different 
strategy for each market, with a focus on operational efficiency, profitability and long-term value 
creation.

owned outlets in Australia and New Zealand compare in terms of sales growth, outlet-level 
profitability and returns on invested capital?

softer performance in New Zealand resulting a better profitability and higher ROI in Australia than 
New Zealand. 
 
The Group remains open to explore suitable growth opportunities in both markets. Future capital 
allocation continues to be guided by amongst others, market conditions, outlet-level profitability 
and expected investment returns, with expansion pursued selectively to support sustainable

governance mechanism for both shareholders to oversee key decisions and the joint venture’s 
operations.

external audit. The Group considers that the existing governance arrangements, segregation of 
responsibilities and joint approval mechanisms and independent external audit provide 
appropriate oversight over the joint venture. The Group will continue to monitor the adequacy of 
these arrangements and assess whether additional assurance measures are required where 
appropriate. 
 
(ii) 
Given that the group’s operations are primarily in Australia and New Zealand, while its 
outsourced internal audit provider appears to be the Singapore-based entity, could the 
company clarify how internal audits are conducted on the ground? Are the audits 
performed by Singapore-based personnel, local teams in Australia and New Zealand, or a 
combination of both?   
 
Response: 
The Group’s internal audits are conducted by Singapore-based personnel from a Singapore-
based outsourced internal audit provider. While there is no local internal audit team based in 
Australia or New Zealand, the audit approach includes on-site fieldwork to Australia and New 
Zealand depending on the scope and nature of the audit, to review the relevant operational 
processes and internal controls.  Accordingly, the internal audit team adopts a combination of 
Singapore-based audit planning and oversight, together with on-site fieldwork in Australia and 
New Zealand. 
(iii) 
How does the IA bridge any gaps in local knowledge of Australia and New Zealand, where 
regulatory requirements, business practices and workplace cultures may differ from 
Singapore, while meeting the internal audit standards and governance expectations 
applicable to an SGX-listed company? 
 
Response: 
 
The IA team is based in Singapore and undertakes the necessary research and familiarisation 
with the relevant laws, regulations and business practices applicable to the Group’s operations 
in Australia and New Zealand. The team also engages with local management to understand the 
local operating environment and, where necessary, seeks input from relevant subject matter 
experts to validate its understanding of applicable requirements. 
 
All reviews are conducted using a consistent risk-based internal audit methodology aligned with 
the International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing and the governance 
expectations of an SGX-listed company. This includes assessing the adequacy and effectiveness 
of internal controls, risk management processes and compliance frameworks, while taking into 
consideration both SGX governance requirements and local regulatory obligations. 
 
(iv)

Response: 
 
The FY2026 internal audit covered three outlets in Australia and New Zealand and reviewed key 
business processes, including Sales to Collection, Procurement, Payables and Payment, Fixed 
Assets and Inventory Management, Human Resources and Payroll, together with an internal 
review of selected environmental, social and governance (“ESG”) matters.
